title: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar
hook: a first meeting with someone who knows more: the Gita gives three moves
carry: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar

segments.voice: Yesterday, the graduate's path began in water: the snataka bathes, and walks home with everything learned. Today the graduate goes looking for a teacher again.

A first meeting with someone who knows far more than you do: a new boss, a professor, a coach, the grandmother of a friend. There are two easy mistakes. Act like you already know it all, so they'll take you seriously. Or sit there silent, nodding, too polite to ask anything real. The Bhagavad Gita has a verse for this exact meeting, and it gives three moves.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO KNOWS MORE.` → `TWO EASY MISTAKES.` → `THE GITA: THREE MOVES.`

segments.voice: Krishna tells Arjuna how to learn from the wise. Learn it, he says, by bowing down, by asking, by serving. The wise, who have seen the truth, will teach you. Three Sanskrit words. Pranipata: bowing down, a body bent toward the person. Pariprashna: asking, all the way around a thing, the full set of questions. Seva: service, being useful to the one who teaches. Look at the middle word. The posture the Gita describes isn't silent awe. It's bowing, and then asking hard, and then helping. The respect makes room for the questions instead of shutting them down. The Mundaka Upanishad pictures the same meeting with one detail: the seeker goes to a teacher fuel in hand, carrying firewood for the teacher's fire. You arrive bringing something useful, not just a need. So the graduate's path doesn't end the learning. It changes the classroom. After the bath, the graduate keeps finding people who know more, and walks up to them the old way: bowed, curious, and carrying a little wood.
screen: `BOW, ASK, SERVE.` · `PARIPRASHNA: ASK ALL THE WAY.` · `FUEL IN HAND.` · `THE CLASSROOM CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, the way you'd hold something out to a teacher. Lower your head a little, toward no one in particular, and notice how the breath changes. Then lift your head as if about to ask a question, and stay there, open and curious, for the rest of the sit.
The graduate's path: after study, finding the wise again, and meeting them the Gita's way, bowing, asking, serving.
Your line: the graduate's path — a Keeper seminar. Come bowed, come curious, come with some wood. That's today.

screen: `DAY 1783 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 7 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: WHO TAUGHT YOUR TEACHER'S TEACHER?`

chat.says: got an interview for a summer program with a professor friday. do i act smart or admit i'm lost?
options: go respectful, ask your real questions, offer to help: the Gita's bow, ask, serve.
act smart. the Gita says the wise teach only students who already know a lot.
just listen and nod. in the Gita, questions to a teacher come off as rude.
chat.meaning: Gita 4.34: learn by bowing down, by asking, by serving. Respect and real questions go together, and you bring something useful.

pranipata.meaning: bowing down: the first of the Gita's three moves

pariprashna.meaning: thorough questioning: asking all the way around

seva.meaning: service, being useful to the one who teaches
